add.issue.name: A killed fetch leaves a remote-ref lock that wedges every later sync

edit.description.md:
`QR97TP3` clears `refs/heads/<stateBranch>.lock` from the common git directory, but not the sibling lock a killed *fetch* leaves there.

`git.fetch` (`git-commands.ts:59`) runs `+refs/heads/<b>:refs/remotes/origin/<b>` with `cwd = stateBranchRoot`, so a SIGKILL or SIGTERM during it leaves `refs/remotes/origin/<stateBranch>.lock` behind, and every later sync dies in `pullWithRebase` with `cannot lock ref 'refs/remotes/origin/epiq/state'`. That is the identical permanent wedge `QR97TP3` repaired, at a likelier kill point: the fetch is the longest git call in a sync, and the 10s cap SIGTERMs it by design.

`refs/remotes/<origin>/<branch>` is as unambiguously epiq's as the branch itself, so the same named-ref rule can clear it.

From a review of PR #388.

add.issue.name: The state branch's ref lock is deleted without anything establishing it is stale

edit.description.md:
`clearStaleGitLocks` (`git-utils.ts:726`) deletes `refs/heads/<stateBranch>.lock` on the strength of the sync lock's pid being dead. Nothing establishes the ref lock itself is stale, and the name promises a check the body does not make.

The scenario `QR97TP3`'s own harness change acknowledges — a node process SIGKILLed while its spawned `git` survives, which is why the test now kills the process group — produces a live orphaned `git commit` still holding that lock. The next epiq process finds the pid dead, claims `dead`, deletes the live lock and commits; the orphan then renames its own lock into place and the newer commit is dropped from the branch. Committed events with no ref left pointing at them.

The worktree-scoped `clearStaleGitLocks` confines this to a worktree epiq owns; this one reaches the shared ref store, where the failure is a lost update rather than a refused command. An mtime guard — skip a lock younger than a few seconds — would keep the wedge fix and close this.

`sync-recovery.test.ts:465` covers another branch's lock only; nothing covers a live holder of the state branch's.

From a review of PR #388.

add.issue.name: killed-sync no longer kills mid-sync, and its guard cannot tell

edit.description.md:
`P5VM0FE` moved the kill, but past the window rather than into it.

With `killAfterSyncStartMs: 0` (`killed-sync.test.ts:95`) the kill lands ~1–6 ms after the actor touches the marker — a 5 ms poll plus a 0 ms timer — which is inside `ensureSyncReady`, before any fetch, rebase or commit has run. The round setup at lines 70–80, six `runActor` syncs per round explicitly "work for ana's rebase to be partway through when it dies", now serves nothing, and the file's stated subject — recovery from the rebase and autostash a mid-sync death leaves — is exercised in no round, while the run still pays for 48 publishing syncs. The old timing missed by landing after the sync; this one misses by landing before it.

`diedMidSync` (`harness.ts:401`) cannot catch that: it only proves the actor got past `actor.ts:116`, which is written *before* `syncEpiqWithRemote` is called. So the guard the change advertises — "a kill that lands nowhere no longer passes quietly" — accepts a kill that landed nowhere, and rejects only one that landed after the whole run.

A ramp measured from the marker (say `round * 40` ms against the 186–451 ms sync the comment cites) would land inside for most rounds; a second marker written after the sync's first git command, or an assertion on state the sync left behind, would pin the premise.

From a review of PR #388.

add.issue.name: The killed-sync kill races the actor's own exit, and fails the run blaming the wrong thing

edit.description.md:
`harness.ts:377` kills the actor on a 5 ms poll plus a timer. If ana's sync returns quickly — refusing with "Another process is syncing", a refusal `killed-sync.test.ts:128` explicitly filters for, so one that does occur in this suite — the actor falls through to `fs.writeFileSync(job.reportPath, …)` (`actor.ts:153`) and exits before the kill fires.

`diedMidSync` is then false and line 101 fails the whole 900 s test with "ana's sync was still running when it was killed in round N", which points away from the cause. The report that would explain it is on disk and never read.

Reading the report when `diedMidSync === false` and surfacing its `problems`, then retrying the round rather than failing, would turn this into a retry instead of a red suite.

From a review of PR #388.

add.issue.name: The GUI warnings run fails on ticket-panel timeouts, three runs in four

edit.description.md:
`GUI warnings` (the `EPIQ_GUI_DEV_BUILD=1` run from `ZMD98G5`) has failed three of the four times it has ever run, always the same way: an `addTicket` helper times out on `expect(page.locator('aside')).toContainText(title)` with "element(s) not found" — the ticket panel never arrives after the ticket is filed.

Which tests it hits moves around, which is what says it is the run and not the tests:

- run 35501089859 (09:00, before the worker cap): `scatter-gesture`, `ref-preview`, `scrubber-persistence`
- run 35510359120 (12:21, after it): `tab-persistence:97`, `event-log:766`, `ticket-window:318`

Capping the workers (`ZMD98G5`) made it green once and did not fix it. The development bundle is 2.7 MB against the production one, so the board takes longer to become interactive than Playwright's default expect timeout allows on a four-vCPU runner — the same slowness the cap was aimed at, not yet far enough.

Worth trying: a longer `expect` timeout for this run (`EPIQ_E2E_TIMEOUT_SCALE` already exists for the node e2e), or waiting on something the board raises when it is ready rather than on the panel's text.

It is noise either way: a job that is red most of the time stops being read, and this one exists to catch React warnings that the production bundle strips.

add.issue.comment.md:
Solution: PR #392, commits `feb14db1` and `56039d29`. Not a timeout — a lost reply.

The socket URL carried the board, so the effect listed `boardId` and rebuilt the connection whenever it changed, including the first time, when the app boots at `/` and redirects a moment later. The run's own trace has it: `ws://…/ws` at 12:27:06.218Z, `ws://…/ws?boardId=HQTGPJA` at 12:27:07.744Z — ~170ms after the test pressed Enter. `issues:create` went out on the first socket, the broadcast drew the ticket's card on the second, and `issues:create:result`, the only thing that opens the panel, came back to a socket that had gone. Hence a created ticket, no panel, no console error, a URL that never changed. The actions either side took 146–492ms; nothing was slow.

The server has never read that parameter — `git log -S` says it only ever existed in the client — so the fix is a deletion, and one socket now lasts the session. Nothing rested on the swap: the history refetch lists `boardId` in its own deps, and `state:get` on open is workspace-wide. Every board switch had been silently reconnecting; `navigateRef` exists because the same bug one level down tore the socket down on every ticket switch.

Reviewing that turned up what the swap had been hiding: `contributors:get` is board-scoped, answering it replays the event log, and its reply carried no board and was applied unconditionally — the dying socket is what used to discard a stale one. It echoes its `boardId` now, the way `timeline` echoes its request id. `issues:create:result` also still navigated on the route's own `boardId`, empty until the redirect commits; it uses `boardSlug` like the rest of the file.

`socket-lifetime.pw.ts` counts sockets across the redirect and two board switches, verified red without the fix and printing the same pair as CI. Not covered: the contributors guard — driving it wants websocket interception plus an assignee picker with no test ids.

Full GUI e2e 208 passed on the production bundle and 208 on the development one, 2056 unit tests, tsc and eslint clean, gate green before merge.
